Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

hey, can you turn these notes and coordinator messages into a practical volunteer event plan for Alder Wharf Community Garden’s tool-share day? The event is Sunday 18 October. We need something volunteers can use on the day, not a promotional announcement or a recap of what happened. Keep the event name as “Alder Wharf Tool-Share Day.”

The main work is sorting 40 donated hand tools, repairing handles on 12 tools, and labeling 20 items for the garden’s loan shelf. Those numbers are from the coordinators’ notes; they haven’t said whether the 12 repairs and 20 labels overlap with the 40 tools, so don’t imply that they’re separate groups. They do want a simple schedule and an indication of who is responsible for the jobs, but only assign roles where the messages give us a person or a clear group. Don’t fill in gaps with made-up volunteers.

Nia’s message from Monday: “I’ll have the Gate B key and the first-aid kit from the shed. Please keep the paved loading lane clear; the delivery trolley needs to get through at 8:30, before we put the sorting tables out.” She also says there are three raised beds beside the tool shed and that the public entrance is Gate B, not the garden’s side path. The loading lane is paved, but the ground beyond it can be muddy if it has rained. Nobody has confirmed a rain forecast or a wet-weather venue, so don’t treat either as settled.

Sam’s message: “We have 18 confirmed volunteers. Five more people have said they might come, but please don’t count them as confirmed.” Sam can lead the tool sorting and has two folding tables in the shed. He asks for a check-in list at the entrance, but the notes don’t say who will hold it. He expects the public to arrive during the session and wants the loan-shelf items kept apart from tools that still need work. There is no count of public visitors.

Jo’s message: “I can show people how to replace a loose handle, but I can’t supervise every repair station at once.” Jo has a small box of replacement screws and two wooden handles; the notes do not say these are enough for all 12 repairs. Jo says volunteers should not use power tools unless a coordinator is present. Nobody has yet confirmed that any power tools will be brought, or who would operate them. Please retain that distinction rather than turn it into a guarantee that tools are available or prohibited in every circumstance.

Other site and task notes: the shed has the donated tools and two folding tables, but the shed key is not listed separately from Nia’s Gate B key. There is one shared 15-metre extension lead. Two volunteers offered to bring their own cordless drills, but neither name is in the messages. There are work gloves in mixed sizes, though nobody counted them. The group has masking tape and thick markers for labeling. No one has confirmed how many bins or trays are available, and there is no stated plan for disposing of broken items. Keep those as unconfirmed details rather than supplying an answer.

A few access notes from Sam: Bus 6 stops about two blocks from Gate B. Street parking nearby is limited; he does not know how many spaces will be free on Sunday. There is no reserved parking or accessible parking information in the messages. The paved lane must remain clear for the delivery trolley, so it shouldn’t be presented as volunteer parking or a gathering spot. Please include the transport details without promising that parking will be available.

Refreshments are not arranged. Nia says the garden tap is working, but no one has checked whether drinking cups or bottled water will be brought. The notes mention a first-aid kit in the shed with Nia; they do not name a first aider or give an emergency contact number. Volunteers should be told where the kit is according to that message, but don’t assign a medical role that hasn’t been agreed. Also, no one has supplied an accessibility contact, a safeguarding procedure, or a process for recording incidents.

We need the final plan to cover the day’s timings, arrival and check-in, the tool sorting/repair/labeling work, named coordinator responsibilities, what supplies are known to be on site, and the access and safety points that are actually in these notes. A short section called “Still to confirm” would help keep the missing details visible, especially the check-in volunteer, the possible drill use, the number of gloves, the bins or trays, refreshments and any wet-weather arrangement. Don’t turn possibilities into commitments, and don’t add a role for a person unless the messages support it.

For the timings, use 8:15 arrival, the 8:30 delivery trolley access, 9:30 public opening, 1:00 end of the public session and 1:30 expected pack-up finish. No one has supplied individual break times or a more detailed task rotation, so don’t invent exact breaks or a full staffing roster. Sam’s sorting lead role and Jo’s limited repair demonstration are the only clearly stated work assignments; the plan can make that limitation plain. Keep the three raised beds and the tool shed as location details, not as extra work tasks.

There’s also a communication note from Nia: “If anyone asks about borrowing tools, explain that the labeled items are for the loan shelf, but we haven’t written the borrowing rules yet.” No borrowing period, deposit, return process or eligibility rule has been agreed. Include the quote as coordinator guidance and make sure the plan does not invent loan rules. The event is called a tool-share day, but we’re not asking you to create a new lending policy.

Please organize the information so the coordinators can check it quickly, using a numbered section if that makes sense. Keep the supplied coordinator messages and their wording in the prompt rather than collapsing them into a short summary, and use ordinary paragraphs around them. The plan itself should be concise enough to use at the garden, while the unanswered items remain visible. Cover timings, arrival and check-in, sorting, repair and labeling work, named coordinator responsibilities, known on-site supplies, access, and the safety points supported by the notes.
